tldr: The authors propose "ChainSplat," a framework that models deformable linear objects (DLOs) like ropes and cables as open-chain structures connected by revolute joints, jointly learning their 3D geometry, appearance, kinematics, and dynamics parameters solely from multi-view RGB videos. Its low-dimensional, physically consistent representation enables accurate dynamics prediction and rendering, while also facilitating real-time state estimation and trajectory optimization for target-striking tasks.
hero_caption: Shows the four core components of ChainSplat: Link-aware Gaussians with link membership probabilities, Screw joints defining revolute axes and spring-damper properties, Link inertial parameters (mass, inertia, friction), and the driving Joint configuration.
overview:
Deformable linear objects (DLOs) such as cables and ropes are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate accurately. This difficulty stems from their massive configuration spaces and the intricate interplay of unknown material properties like stiffness and friction. While building physics-based digital twins from video has gained traction, existing approaches rely on multi-stage pipelines that reconstruct tens of thousands of 3D particles from 2D tracking and depth images. These pipelines are brittle under dynamic interactions due to depth noise, and their high state dimensionality makes real-time control and state estimation computationally intractable.

To overcome this, the authors turned to a classic robotic concept: open-chain mechanisms based on screw theory. By treating a DLO as a serial-link system where rigid links are connected by revolute joints, they compress the system's state space into a super-compact joint angle vector with just a handful of parameters. By pairing each link with 3D Gaussians that carry link membership probabilities (3D Gaussian Splatting), they built "ChainSplat"—a framework that end-to-end and differentiably identifies appearance, geometry, kinematics, and dynamics solely from multi-view RGB videos.

Evaluated on a real-world humanoid robot arm across tabletop friction and airborne gravity settings, ChainSplat significantly outperformed existing particle-based digital twin baselines (PhysTwin and PGND) in both dynamics prediction accuracy and rendering quality. Furthermore, leveraging its differentiable dynamics, the team demonstrated gradient-based trajectory optimization for target-striking tasks, as well as real-time state and external force estimation from a single monocular camera on real hardware.
contributions: Mathematically modeled DLOs as screw-theoretic open-chain mechanisms and integrated them with 3D Gaussian Splatting to unify geometry, appearance, and dynamics solely from RGB videos.

Constructed a two-stage optimization pipeline combining differentiable rendering with link-probability replication and asynchronous resets for kinematics estimation, followed by implicit Euler integration for dynamics identification.

Leveraged the learned compact, differentiable physics model to demonstrate real-time state and external force estimation from RGB video and gradient-based trajectory optimization for dynamic manipulation on real robots.

sections.heading: How should we model DLOs? A paradigm shift from particle clouds to mechanisms
sections.summary: Learning DLO dynamics requires balancing accurate 3D geometry and appearance acquisition with a compact state representation suitable for control. This chapter highlights the computational burden and depth-dependency issues of existing particle-based methods, introducing the core idea behind ChainSplat: fusing screw-theoretic open-chain mechanisms with Gaussian Splatting.
sections.details:
Deformable linear objects (DLOs) such as cables and hoses are ubiquitous across daily and industrial environments, yet manipulating them accurately remains challenging. They exhibit high-dimensional deformation spaces, and their physical properties are typically unknown beforehand.

Recent efforts have focused on building digital twins of deformable objects from video. However, most prior methods (such as PhysTwin) adopt multi-stage pipelines: they back-project 2D tracking results with depth maps to create thousands of 3D particles, skin these particles to capture deformation, and then render RGB images. This paradigm suffers from two fatal weaknesses:
- First is the "reliance on depth images." Under fast, dynamic interactions, depth sensors suffer from severe noise, compounding errors across the entire pipeline.
- Second is the "explosion of state dimensionality." Managing thousands to tens of thousands of particles in the state space makes forward simulation heavy, rendering model predictive control and real-time filtering computationally prohibitive.

To address this, the authors introduce "ChainSplat." It treats the DLO as an open-chain system composed of multiple rigid links connected by revolute joints. Geometry and appearance are represented by 3D Gaussians tied to each link, while kinematics and dynamics are analytically modeled using robotics screw theory. This keeps the state vector $\bm{\theta}$ extremely compact while enabling end-to-end, differentiable identification of geometry, appearance, and physical parameters entirely from multi-view RGB videos.

sections.heading: Neural dynamics and physics-informed models: Progress and limitations
sections.summary: Methods for predicting deformable object behavior broadly fall into pure neural networks and physics-informed approaches. This chapter reviews the evolution of both paradigms and clarifies ChainSplat's role in simultaneously achieving geometry/appearance reconstruction and a control-friendly, low-dimensional physics model.
sections.details:
Research into DLO dynamics modeling has evolved alongside developments in representations.

### II-A Neural Dynamics Models for Deformable Linear Objects
Early works used CNNs to predict deformations directly in image space, but recent approaches focus on representing objects as graphs or point clouds. Models have been proposed using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to propagate inter-particle interactions, Transformers to capture long-term deformation, and bidirectional LSTMs to track DLO endpoint coordinates. However, because these data-driven neural models do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws or geometric constraints, they easily overfit to training distributions and struggle to generalize to unseen robot motions.

### II-B Physics-Informed Dynamics Models
To embed physical laws as inductive biases, methods based on Discrete Elastic Rods (DER) and Pseudo-Rigid-Body (PRB) formulations have been proposed. PRB models DLOs as articulated mechanisms, making them low-dimensional and well-suited for control; however, they focus purely on dynamics identification and do not address reconstructing 3D geometry or appearance from video.

Conversely, recent frameworks such as PhysTwin, PGND, and EMPM can build photorealistic digital twins from interaction videos using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Yet, as noted earlier, they rely on thousands of 3D particles as their base units and require depth-camera tracking and multi-stage pipelines, making control applications exceptionally difficult. ChainSplat bridges this gap by integrating a compact, mechanism-based low-dimensional physics model like PRB with the high-fidelity rendering of Gaussian Splatting.

sections.heading: The mathematical toolkit: Screw theory, open-chain dynamics, and 3D Gaussian Splatting
sections.summary: This chapter explains the three foundational mathematical pillars of the proposed method: forward kinematics using Lie group screw theory on SE(3), manipulator dynamics derived via the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm, and differentiable rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting.
sections.details:
The mathematical foundation of ChainSplat merges robot kinematics with modern computer vision.

### III-A Kinematics of Open-Chain Systems and Screw Theory
Rigid-body poses are represented on the special Euclidean group $\text{SE}(3)$. An element of its Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ is called a twist $\bm{S}=(\bm{\omega},\bm{v})$, containing an angular velocity $\bm{\omega}$ and a linear velocity $\bm{v}$. Using screw theory, rigid-body transformations driven by a joint displacement $\theta$ can be expressed in closed form via the matrix exponential $e^{[\bm{S}]\theta}$. The forward kinematics of an open chain with $n$ serial joints is formulated by the Product of Exponentials (PoE) formula:

$$\bm{T}(\bm{\theta}) = e^{[\bm{S}_1]\theta_1} \cdots e^{[\bm{S}_n]\theta_n} \bm{T}(\bm{0})$$

### III-B Dynamics of Open-Chain Systems
The equations of motion for each link are formulated via the adjoint map $\text{Ad}_{\bm{T}}$ and the small adjoint map $\text{ad}_{\bm{S}}$. By applying the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) to propagate spatial velocities and wrenches (forces/torques $\bm{F}\in\mathfrak{se}(3)^*$) between links, the standard manipulator equation of motion (Eq. 19)—including the inertia matrix $\bm{M}(\bm{\theta})$, Coriolis and centrifugal terms $\bm{C}(\bm{\theta},\dot{\bm{\theta}})$, and gravity $\bm{g}(\bm{\theta})$—is derived in closed form.

### III-C 3D Gaussian Splatting
The scene is parameterized as a collection of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a center position $\bm{\mu}$, rotation $\bm{R}$, anisotropic scale $\bm{s}$, opacity $\sigma$, and color $\bm{c}$ parameterized by spherical harmonics. By sorting Gaussians along the viewing ray and performing alpha blending, RGB images can be rendered in a fully differentiable manner.

captions.F3: Link coordinate frames and data flow of the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm. Velocities and accelerations are propagated forward from base to tip, while forces and moments are propagated backward from tip to base to calculate joint torques.

sections.heading: ChainSplat formulation: Embedding Gaussians into articulated structures
sections.summary: This chapter defines the model structure of ChainSplat for a robot-grasped DLO. It details the design of Gaussians carrying link membership probabilities, the Gaussian replication scheme that enables smooth optimization, and the equation of motion incorporating base motion, viscous friction, and spring-dampers.
sections.details:
We consider a setting where a robot grasps and manipulates the base of a DLO. The base link follows the robot end-effector trajectory $\bm{T}_b(t)$.

### IV-A ChainSplat Components
ChainSplat consists of four primary components (Fig. F4):
- **Screw joints $\mathcal{S}_j$**: Defined by screw axis $\bm{S}_j$, passive torsional spring stiffness $\kappa_j$, and damping coefficient $d_j$.
- **Link inertial parameters $\mathcal{M}_j$**: Link mass $m_j$, rotational inertia matrix $\bm{I}_j$, and ground friction coefficient $\mu_j$.
- **Link-aware Gaussians $\mathcal{H}_i$**: Along with standard Gaussian parameters, each carries a probability distribution $\bm{\rho}_i \in \Delta^{n_s}$ indicating its link membership.
- **Joint configuration $\bm{\theta}_k$**: The joint angle vector describing the DLO's deformation state at time step $k$.

### IV-B Differentiable RGB Rendering
Directly assigning each Gaussian to its most probable link (hard assignment) makes the process non-differentiable with respect to $\bm{\rho}_i$ and prone to poor local minima. Instead, ChainSplat replicates each Gaussian $\mathcal{H}_i$ into $(n_s+1)$ Gaussians $\mathcal{G}_{ij}$, one for each link (Fig. F5). Each replica transforms according to link $j$'s kinematics, with its opacity weighted by the membership probability $\rho_{ij}$. This allows gradients from image rendering losses to flow smoothly into joint angles $\bm{\theta}_k$ and probabilities $\bm{\rho}_i$.

### IV-C Dynamics Model Extensions
To account for base accelerations $\dot{\bm{V}}_b$ induced by the robot gripper, forward propagation is initialized with $\dot{\bm{V}}_0 = (\bm{0}, -\bm{g}) + \dot{\bm{V}}_b$. In addition, passive torques $\tau_j = -\kappa_j\theta_j - d_j\dot{\theta}_j$ are added to joints, and translational viscous friction $\bm{\mu}_i\bm{V}_i$ is incorporated for tabletop contact. Combining these yields closed-form equations of motion (Eq. 40) containing dynamic coupling terms $\bm{M}_0, \bm{C}_0$ with the base motion.

captions.F5: Replication mechanism for link-aware Gaussians. A single Gaussian is transformed to different candidate poses following each link's kinematics, with each replica's opacity scaled by the membership probability $\rho_{ij}$, enabling differentiable rendering and smooth optimization.

sections.heading: Two-stage optimization framework: From geometric reconstruction to physics identification
sections.summary: This chapter details the two-stage optimization procedure to learn all ChainSplat parameters from multi-view RGB videos. Stage 1 reconstructs geometry, appearance, and joint trajectories end-to-end, while Stage 2 identifies physical parameters like mass and damping using implicit Euler integration.
sections.details:
Jointly optimizing geometry, kinematics, and dynamics in one go often leads to divergence. Therefore, the framework adopts a fully differentiable two-stage approach.

### V-A Kinematics-Aware Geometric Perception (Stage 1)
First, geometry, appearance, and joint trajectories are recovered from RGB videos. Freely optimizing screw axes $\bm{S}_j$ alongside all other parameters often caused joints to settle into physically unrealistic configurations; hence, a geometric constraint is imposed by fixing the axes at equal intervals pointing in the same direction (providing high stability for planar deformation tasks).

Optimization minimizes the photometric rendering loss (Eq. 31) against SAM-masked RGB images. To avoid local minima, the authors introduce a "periodic link-probability reset" alongside the standard 3DGS opacity resets. Running these two resets on an asynchronous schedule allows Gaussians to cleanly separate and assign themselves to the correct links. A key output of this stage is the time-series joint angle trajectory $\bm{\theta}_k$.

### V-B Dynamics Parameter Identification (Stage 2)
Using the extracted joint angle trajectories $\bm{\theta}_k$ as ground truth, the damping coefficients $d_j$, link masses $m_j$, and friction coefficients $\mu_j$ are identified by minimizing the squared error against simulated trajectories $\hat{\bm{\theta}}_k$ (Eq. 51).

When simulating at coarse time steps around 30 Hz, explicit Euler integration easily becomes numerically unstable due to velocity-dependent terms (damping and friction). ChainSplat instead adopts an "implicit Euler scheme (first-order Taylor expansion in velocity)." Crucially, because ChainSplat's formulation allows the velocity Jacobian of acceleration $\partial a(\dot{\bm{\theta}})/\partial\dot{\bm{\theta}}$ to be derived analytically in closed form (Eq. 48), implicit simulation runs exceptionally fast and stably without numerical differentiation.

sections.heading: Putting the model to work: Trajectory optimization, real-time tracking, and force estimation
sections.summary: This chapter discusses downstream applications of the learned ChainSplat model. It details gradient-based trajectory optimization for target-striking tasks enabled by differentiability, rapid joint state estimation from a monocular RGB camera, and external force estimation via contact Jacobians under human interaction.
sections.details:
Leveraging the model's low dimensionality and differentiable rendering capabilities, three practical applications were developed.

### VI-A Model-Based Trajectory Optimization
The objective is a dynamic task where the DLO's tip or body must strike a spatial target point $\bm{p}_d$ (Fig. F6). The 1D end-effector trajectory is parameterized using Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) similar to dynamic movement primitives, optimizing the weight vector $\bm{w}$.
- **Tabletop setting**: A cost function (Eq. 55) is designed so that any point on the DLO reaches the target and comes smoothly to rest at the final time step.
- **Airborne setting**: A cost function (Eq. 56) is designed to leverage gravity-driven swings so that the DLO tip sweeps through the target point at some instant during the motion.

Because ChainSplat provides closed-form, fully differentiable dynamics, optimal trajectories can be searched rapidly via gradient descent.

### VI-B Real-Time State Estimation from Monocular RGB
While multi-view video is used for training, inference requires only a single monocular RGB camera. Joint angles $\bm{\theta}$ are updated via gradient descent to minimize the photometric error between the incoming frame and the ChainSplat rendering (Eq. 57). Using the previous frame's estimate as an initialization allows convergence in just a few iterations.

### VI-C External Force Estimation
Contact forces can be estimated without force sensors when a human pushes or pulls the DLO. Assuming the gripper is stationary and deformations are quasi-static, the joint torque balance is given by $\bm{J}^T \bm{F}_{\text{ext}} = \bm{K}\bm{\theta} + \bm{g}(\bm{\theta})$. Using real-time estimated joint angles and the pseudo-inverse of the contact Jacobian $\bm{J}$ (derived from image-detected contact points), the external force vector $\bm{f}_{\text{ext}}$ (Eq. 59) is computed analytically.

captions.F6: Illustration of the objective functions for target-striking manipulation. Left: Point cloud model extracted from ChainSplat. Right: Optimization framework driving the entire body (tabletop) or the tip point cloud (airborne) toward the target point $\bm{p}_d$.

sections.heading: Real-world experiments and benchmarks: From dynamics rollouts to striking tasks
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on a humanoid robot arm manipulating ropes of three different lengths. ChainSplat achieved SOTA performance against baselines (PGND, PhysTwin) in both dynamics prediction and appearance rendering, while also validating monocular tracking, force estimation, and target striking with sub-centimeter accuracy.
sections.details:
### VII-A Experimental Setup
The setup comprised the left arm of an RB-Y1 humanoid robot (parallel gripper) and three RealSense D435 cameras (Fig. F7). Experiments evaluated ropes of lengths 20 cm, 30 cm, and 40 cm (thickness 2 cm) across two environments: tabletop (friction-dominated) and airborne (gravity-dominated). Baselines included MPM-based PGND and mass-spring-based PhysTwin (both with and without its 3D reconstruction module).

### VII-B Dynamics Prediction and Digital Twin Modeling Accuracy
Evaluations measured geometric accuracy (Chamfer Distance: CD, IoU) and visual rendering quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) of predicted rope states.
- **Tabletop setting (Fig. F8, Table I)**: ChainSplat substantially outperformed baselines in visual metrics. In geometric accuracy (CD), it matched PhysTwin—which directly consumes depth inputs—while using only RGB video.
- **Airborne setting (Fig. F9, Table II)**: In gravity-dominated motions, ChainSplat's advantages were even more pronounced, dominating baselines across all metrics and rope lengths. PGND failed completely under dynamic gravity swings, and PhysTwin exhibited large tracking errors.
- **Computational Efficiency (Table III)**: ChainSplat required the shortest training time per trajectory at 17.6 minutes (9.2 min for geometry + 8.4 min for dynamics) and achieved the fastest inference speeds for both physical simulation and RGB rendering.

### VII-C State Estimation and Force Estimation Evaluation
In human-rope interaction scenes, combining monocular RGB inputs with SAM2 segmentation (5–6 Hz) and gradient-based optimization (10 iterations, 2–3 Hz) achieved robust tracking. In addition, external force vectors accounting for gravity and surface friction were estimated with physically consistent directions and magnitudes.

### VII-D Real-Robot Manipulation Results
Target-striking tasks were validated using the optimized gripper trajectories (Fig. F12). Intriguingly, the optimized motions automatically reflected physical properties: producing quick, short motions for the 20 cm rope, and wide, relaxed pendulum swings for the 40 cm rope matching its lower natural frequency. While an unoptimized model without dynamics identification (ChainSplat w/o dyn) missed targets widely, the fully optimized ChainSplat struck targets accurately with an average error below 1 cm (Table IV).

captions.F7: Real-world experimental setup. The gripper of the RB-Y1 humanoid robot holds the rope, captured by three multi-view RealSense cameras. Left: Tabletop environment. Right: Airborne environment.
captions.F8: Comparison of dynamics rollouts in the tabletop setting. Over time, PGND drifts even at the grasped base, and PhysTwin displays shape distortion, whereas ChainSplat tracks ground-truth video most accurately.

sections.heading: Discussion and future avenues: Toward end-to-end learning and adaptive control
sections.summary: This chapter addresses the structural bias inherent in the current two-stage optimization and explores the potential for truly end-to-end unified kinodynamic learning. It also envisions designing optimal excitation trajectories for varied objects and extending toward online adaptive, closed-loop control.
sections.details:
Building upon their findings, the authors outline three promising directions for future research:

### VIII-1 Moving to Full End-to-End Optimization
In the current two-stage approach, estimation errors and biases from the first stage (geometry and kinematics) propagate directly into the second stage (dynamics identification). Unifying kinodynamic learning by optimizing kinematic parameters (such as joint axis placement) and dynamics parameters within a single loop could eliminate geometric redundancies and yield more accurate identification.

### VIII-2 Generalization Across Objects and Optimal Excitation Trajectories
To adapt to diverse materials and lengths, incorporating "optimal excitation trajectories" from robotic control is more effective than merely collecting random data. Automatically designing gripper motions that maximize information gain for dynamics identification could allow highly accurate models to be learned from minimal data. Coupling this with adaptive control to update physical parameters online during manipulation is another promising avenue.

### VIII-3 Real-Time Closed-Loop Reactive Control
While the current manipulation demonstration operates open-loop, pairing ChainSplat's ultra-compact state space with its fast state estimator paves the way toward real-time model predictive control (MPC) capable of reactive obstacle avoidance and disturbance rejection, as well as zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of policies trained via reinforcement learning in simulation.

sections.heading: Summary: A breakthrough at the intersection of geometry and mechanism theory
sections.summary: This chapter wraps up ChainSplat, which unifies DLO geometry, appearance, and dynamics learning from RGB videos by blending screw-theoretic open-chain models with 3D Gaussian Splatting. Its compact, physically grounded model is expected to serve as a versatile foundation for robotic deformable manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented ChainSplat, a physics-inspired framework that models deformable linear objects (DLOs) as revolute-jointed open-chain mechanisms, integrating screw theory with 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Without relying on noisy, expensive depth maps or multi-stage pipelines typical of particle-based methods, ChainSplat successfully reconstructs 3D geometry, photorealistic appearance, kinematics, and dynamics parameters end-to-end from multi-view RGB videos alone. Beyond setting new state-of-the-art benchmarks in dynamics rollout and rendering quality, it achieves a remarkably compact state space defined by only a few joint variables.

Consequently, the authors demonstrated near-real-time state and contact force estimation from a single monocular camera, as well as rapid gradient-based trajectory optimization for dynamic manipulation on real hardware. This work powerfully illustrates how uniting classical, mathematically rigorous robotic kinematics with modern differentiable rendering can unlock major breakthroughs in deformable object manipulation.

takeaways: Audaciously modeling deformable objects as revolute-jointed open-chain mechanisms dramatically reduces state dimensionality, unlocking exact analytical dynamics simulation and gradient-based control.

Replicating Gaussians across kinematic links and weighting them by membership probabilities (inspired by ScrewSplat) is a powerful paradigm for turning discrete assignment problems into smooth, differentiable optimizations.

Integrating physics simulation into rendering losses via an implicit Euler scheme with closed-form velocity Jacobians prevents divergence, enabling stable dynamics identification even under coarse sampling rates.
limitations: Screw axes are constrained to be collinear and unidirectional, meaning the model cannot currently handle complex 3D out-of-plane twisting or tangling.

Spring stiffness is assumed to be $\kappa_j=0$ for ropes and cables with negligible elasticity, so elastic spring-back behaviors in stiff hoses or metal wires dominated by bending elasticity are not modeled.
Because geometric perception and dynamics identification are split into two sequential stages, systematic errors introduced during the kinematics stage cannot be corrected during dynamics tuning.
